name: Late-Night Call
description: Longfellow lies in bed, still dressed, holding a phone. He makes a call late at night and speaks into the phone, saying he couldn't sleep and wanted to talk, asking if the other person minds.
related_events: Longfellow calls someone late at night unable to sleep

name: Cedar Enters His Private Office
description: Cedar walks through the room and approaches a door labeled 'JOHN CEDAR, PRIVATE.' He opens it and goes inside.
related_events: Cedar passes through the room and enters his private office

name: Babe Confides Insomnia During Late Call
description: Babe is on the phone late at night. Speaking sincerely, Babe says they couldn't sleep either, responding to someone else who had also been awake.
related_events: Babe expresses inability to sleep during phone conversation

name: Guests Arrive in Limousines for Formal Event
description: One by one, black limousines pull up to the entrance of the grand venue under the glow of evening light. Doors open, and guests step out onto the pavement, dressed in elegant evening attire—tailcoats, tuxedos, and flowing gowns. They adjust their cuffs, smooth their dresses, and walk toward the entrance, where soft music and ambient chatter signal the start of the gathering.
related_events: Guests arrive at venue in evening dress

name: Babe Directs Photographers in Taxi Stakeout
description: Babe points out a man in the distance from the back seat of a taxi. She tells Bob and Frank to get their cameras ready and follow her without explaining further. Bob and Frank exchange doubtful remarks, with one calling Babe crazy, but they prepare to move as she exits the cab and moves toward the target.
related_events: Babe identifies target and instructs photographers in taxi
Photographers express skepticism about Babe's plan

name: Cedar Arrives and Enters the Private Office
description: Cedar enters the office and greets the secretary with a morning salutation. He asks where the others are. The secretary responds that they are waiting for him in the other office. Without delay, Cedar crosses the room and goes through a door marked 'PRIVATE,' disappearing inside.
related_events: Cedar arrives and greets secretary
Cedar walks to private office and enters

name: Bob Urges the Taxi Driver to Follow the Bus
description: Bob, one of the photographers, leans out of the taxi window, his head visible as he shouts at the driver. "Hey, flap-ears! You better keep following that bus!" The driver's voice comes from inside the cab, tense but steady. "Keep your shirt on!" The taxi continues moving, staying close behind the bus.
related_events: Photographer Bob leans out of taxi window to shout at driver
Taxi driver responds to Bob's demand while following the bus

name: Longfellow's Emotion Outside Grant's Tomb
description: Longfellow stands across the street from Grant's Tomb, his eyes moist, face solemn. Babe, standing nearby, calls out to him, urging him to come see the monument. She does not appear to notice his emotional state.
related_events: Longfellow shows visible emotion while standing across the street from Grant's Tomb
Babe urges Longfellow to go see Grant's Tomb

name: Switchboard Operator Reports Mr. Cedar's Unavailability
description: The switchboard operator speaks to Mr. Hopper, informing him that Mr. Cedar is not answering his phone. An office clerk passes by and asks what is happening in the boss's office. The operator replies that they don't know, but that the three 'Cs' and little 'B' have been in the office for over an hour.
related_events: Switchboard operator reports Mr. Cedar not answering phone
Office clerk inquires about activity in boss's office
related_occasions: Meeting With The Three 'Cs' And Little 'B'

name: Driver Announces Passenger Exit, Bob and Frank React
description: The taxi driver calls out that a passenger is getting off. Bob and Frank immediately shout for the driver to pull over to the curb.
related_events: Taxi driver alerts passengers about someone getting off
Passengers react with urgency to the stop

name: Bob and Frank Chase the Cab
description: Bob turns to the driver and shouts, 'Hey, stupe! Follow that cab they just got into, will you? Hurry up! Step on it!' Frank leans forward, urging, 'Come on, come on!' Bob repeats his command, 'Hurry up!' The car lurches forward as the pursuit begins. The scene shifts to an electric sign glowing above a restaurant: 'TULLIO'S EAT WITH THE LITERATI'.
related_events: Bob urges driver to chase a cab
Frank urges haste during pursuit
related_occasions: Tullio'S Restaurant Scene

name: Babe and Longfellow Rest on a Park Bench
description: Babe and Longfellow walk together until Babe notices a park bench and gestures toward it. 'Here's a nice place,' he says. Longfellow looks around and replies, 'Yeah. Anyway, there aren't any photographers around.' They sit down on the bench.
related_events: Babe spots a park bench and suggests it as a nice place
Longfellow comments on absence of photographers

name: Babe and Mabel Discuss the Man Who Wants to Carry His Bride
description: Babe talks to Mabel about a man whose traditional ideas unsettle her. She tells Mabel that he said he wants to carry his bride over the threshold when they marry. Babe tries to laugh at the notion but finds she can't. She sits down at her typewriter and says the man has goodness, something she and Mabel have forgotten in their lives. Mabel brushes her off, mentioning Charlie, but Babe remains quiet, lost in thought.
related_events: Babe expresses conflicted feelings about a man's sincerity
Babe reveals man's intention to carry bride over threshold
Babe fails to laugh at man's idealism
Babe reflects on loss of goodness in modern life

name: Longfellow and Cobb Discuss Opera Meetings
description: Longfellow and Cobb step out of a room and begin walking down a corridor. Longfellow remarks that he is busy and asks if opera people always come here for their meetings. Cobb nods and replies, 'Why do mice go where there's cheese?'
related_events: Longfellow and Cobb exit and walk down corridor
Longfellow inquires about opera people's meeting location
Cobb responds with metaphor about mice and cheese
related_occasions: Opera People'S Meeting

name: Babe and Longfellow Visit the Aquarium
description: Babe and Longfellow walk through New York, with Babe showing Longfellow around. Longfellow looks around with quiet fascination, taking in the sights. He turns to Babe and says it's awfully nice of him to give the tour. Babe replies that he enjoys it. Longfellow says the Aquarium was swell, and that if he lived in New York, he'd go there every day. Babe nods and says he'd like to go more often too, but he has a job to think of.
related_events: Longfellow expresses appreciation for tour of New York
Longfellow comments on desire to visit Aquarium daily
Babe acknowledges enjoyment of showing Longfellow around
Babe mentions job responsibilities limiting leisure visits

name: Bob and Frank Watch the Bus
description: Bob and Frank sit with their cameras, eyes fixed on the bus ahead. After a while, Bob says it doesn’t look like they’ll get any pictures tonight. Frank doesn’t respond, but the two remain in their seats, still watching.
related_events: Bob and Frank observe the bus with their camera equipment
Bob expresses doubt about getting photographs that night

name: Frank Suggests Repeating the Drunk Strategy
description: Bob and Frank sit with their cameras, watching the bus ahead. After a long wait, Bob remarks that they probably won’t get any pictures tonight. Frank replies that Babe should get him drunk again.
related_events: Frank suggests getting Babe to intoxicate someone again

name: Wife Confronts George Over Inheritance and Slaps His Newspaper
description: George sits in a chair reading a newspaper, his face marked by dark pouches under his eyes and a twitching nose. His wife paces around him, berating him for not securing the inheritance from his uncle. She calls him a yokel and shouts that he must have been mad to leave the money to someone else when George was just as closely related. George remains silent, only twitching his nose. The wife slaps the newspaper in his hands, demanding to know what he got. He tells her to stop yelling, saying he can't help it if his uncle didn't like him. She reminds him she told him to be nice, and that they've waited ten years for the old man to die so they could live comfortably. George snaps at her to shut up, calling her a nuisance. She replies that she will keep being a nuisance until she gets her hands on some of the money.
related_events: Wife confronts George about inherited money
Wife slaps newspaper George is reading

name: George Stands Up to His Wife After Inheritance News
description: George sits in a chair reading a newspaper when his wife begins circling him, accusing him of being a yokel and complaining that his uncle left all the money to someone else. She reminds George they waited ten years for the uncle to die, expecting to live on Easy Street. George twitches his nose and tells her to stop yelling, saying he can't help that his uncle didn't like him. His wife slaps the newspaper, demanding to know what he got. George tells her to shut up, calls her a nuisance, and says it's too late. The wife declares she will keep being a nuisance until she gets some of the money.
related_events: George defends himself against wife's accusations
Wife threatens to continue being a nuisance until she receives part of the inheritance

name: Walter Interrupts Longfellow's Tuba Playing
description: Longfellow lies in bed in his pajamas, playing the tuba. Walter enters the room and announces that Madame Pomponi is on the telephone, saying the reception is all set. Longfellow stops playing and glares at him, demanding to know why he was interrupted. When Walter insists it is an urgent call, Longfellow points sharply and orders him to leave. Walter hurries out. Longfellow jumps out of bed and chases him down the grand staircase. At the top of the stairs, Longfellow suddenly stops, struck by a new thought.
related_events: Longfellow plays tuba in bed while wearing pajamas
Walter interrupts Longfellow to report Madame Pomponi's phone call
Longfellow angrily dismisses Walter for interrupting his tuba playing
related_occasions: Reception Organized By Madame Pomponi

name: Longfellow Chases Walter and Has an Idea
description: After playing the tuba in his bedroom, Longfellow chases Walter down the grand staircase. He stops at the top of the stairs, suddenly struck by an idea.
related_events: Longfellow chases Walter down the grand staircase
Longfellow stops at the top of the stairs and has a sudden idea
related_occasions: Reception Organized By Madame Pomponi

name: Longfellow's Farewell at the Train
description: The train stands ready to depart, Longfellow on the observation platform with his tuba in hand, Cedar and Cobb at his sides. In the foreground, the crowd calls out their goodbyes, pressing baskets of fruit into Longfellow's arms. The band plays 'Auld Lang Syne' as the train begins to move. Longfellow waves with a faint smile. 'Goodbye, Mrs. Meredith! Goodbye, Jim! Bye, Buddy! Goodbye, everybody!' He pauses, looking around. 'Gosh, I've got a lot of friends.' Cobb glances up at him, silent, watching his face as the train pulls away.
related_events: Longfellow receives fruit baskets from well-wishers
Band plays 'Auld Lang Syne' during departure
Crowd bids farewell to Longfellow

name: Longfellow Departs on the Train with Cobb
description: The train begins to move as Longfellow stands on the observation platform, waving farewell to the crowd gathered at the station. Baskets of fruit are thrust into his hands as the band plays 'Auld Lang Syne.' He calls out goodbyes to individuals in the crowd—Mrs. Meredith, Jim, Buddy, and others—before pausing, then remarking softly that he has a lot of friends. Beside him, Cobb watches Longfellow's face, his expression quiet and moved. The train pulls away, carrying them forward as the station recedes into the distance.
related_events: Train departs with Longfellow on observation platform
Cobb reacts emotionally to Longfellow's departure

name: Cedar and Cobb Reassure Longfellow After His Inheritance
description: Longfellow sits slumped in his seat, staring up at the ceiling, lost in thought. Cobb sits across from him and opens a snifter, pouring a generous drink. He offers it to Longfellow, who declines without looking. Cedar enters, removes his coat, hat, and cane, and hangs them up. He asks Longfellow if he’d like a cigar, but Longfellow refuses that as well. After a moment of silence, Cedar speaks, telling Longfellow not to worry—managing the fortune will be handled with help, and everything will be taken care of. Longfellow responds that he wasn’t worried about the money. Surprised, Cedar waits. Longfellow says he was wondering where the band would find another tuba player. Cobb, who had just taken a sip of his drink, nearly chokes.
related_events: Cobb offers Longfellow a drink
Cedar offers Longfellow a cigar
Cedar arrives and greets Longfellow and Cobb
Cedar reassures Longfellow about managing the fortune

Cobb nearly chokes on his drink

name: Cedar Enters the Law Office
description: Cedar approaches the office door marked 'CEDAR, CEDAR & BUDINGTON - ENTRANCE.' He opens the door and walks inside.
related_events: Cedar opens the office door and enters the office

name: Men Plot to Exploit Longfellow's Gullibility
description: Eight distinguished men sit around a long table, waiting for Longfellow to arrive. At the head of the table, Mr. Douglas remarks that the young man seems childish and unlikely to resist their request for $180,000. The others murmur in agreement, calling the sum a drop in the bucket and praising the idea. Douglas adds with a wink that they are fortunate Longfellow is so fond of music, revealing he plays the tuba in the town band. One of the men, watching the door, announces Longfellow's approach. The group quickly settles, shuffling in preparation for his entrance.
related_events: Mr. Douglas expresses confidence in persuading Longfellow
group voices agree on the feasibility of the financial request
Mr. Douglas reveals Longfellow's involvement in the town band
related_occasions: Meeting Of Eight Distinguished Men

name: The Men Prepare as Longfellow Arrives
description: One of the men standing near the door notices Longfellow approaching and announces his arrival. The others, seated around the long table, fall silent and begin to shuffle in their seats, adjusting their posture and arranging their belongings. Mr. Douglas, seated at the head of the table, gives a subtle nod. The room quiets in anticipation as all eyes turn toward the entrance.
related_events: One of the men observes Longfellow approaching
Group prepares for Longfellow's arrival
related_occasions: Meeting Of Eight Distinguished Men

name: Longfellow Thanks Babe on the Phone
description: Longfellow calls Babe and thanks her again for going out with him. He tells her he doesn’t know what he’d do without her and says she’s made up for all the fake people he’s met. He speaks warmly, his voice carrying a sense of sincerity and affection.
related_events: Longfellow expresses gratitude during phone call

name: Longfellow Shares a Poem He Wrote About Babe
description: Longfellow tells Babe over the phone that he has been working on a poem about her because he sometimes finds it hard to say how he feels. Babe listens and responds that she would like to read it someday. Longfellow says he might have it finished by the next time they meet and asks if he will see her soon. After she confirms, he says good night, hangs up, and lies back, smiling.
related_events: Longfellow shares he is writing a poem about Babe
Babe expresses interest in reading Longfellow's poem

name: Longfellow Finishes the Call and Reflects on the Conversation
description: Longfellow tells Babe he’s been working on a poem about her and hopes to finish it before they meet again. He asks if they’ll see each other soon and listens to her response. After she agrees, he says, 'Gosh, that's swell, Mary,' and they exchange good nights. He hangs up the phone, lies back, and stares off, quietly absorbed in the moment.
related_events: Longfellow confirms poem progress and anticipates next meeting
Longfellow ends phone call with Babe and reflects emotionally
Babe says good night to Longfellow

name: Cedar Arrives at the Office and Greets Staff
description: Cedar strides across the room with purpose, making his way toward the door marked 'PRIVATE OFFICES.' As he passes, a man calls out, 'Hello, John. Where have you been?' Cedar replies without breaking stride, 'I've been fishing.' He approaches a secretary and says, 'Good morning, Celia.' She responds, 'Good morning, Mr. Cedar.' A group of clerks calls out in unison, 'Good morning, Mr. Cedar!' before he reaches the door and opens it, disappearing inside.

name: Cedar Walks Through the Office
description: Cedar strides across the room toward a door marked 'PRIVATE OFFICES.' As he passes, a secretary looks up from her work. Another greets him with 'Good morning, Mr. Cedar,' and a chorus of clerks echoes the greeting. Cedar continues without stopping, exchanging brief words with a man who calls out to him, then pushes through the door and disappears.
related_events: Secretary looks up from work as Cedar passes

name: Frank and Bob Arrive at Grant's Tomb
description: Frank and Bob arrive near the monument. Frank gestures toward Grant's Tomb and tells Bob to look. Bob turns and, unsure, calls out to the driver, asking if that is indeed the Tomb.
related_events: Frank shows Grant's Tomb to Bob
Bob questions the driver about the location of Grant's Tomb

name: Babe and Longfellow Arrive at Grant's Tomb
description: Babe and Longfellow approach the monument. Babe gestures toward Grant's Tomb and says it's often a letdown for most people. Longfellow responds with quiet intensity, describing the Ohio farm boy who became a great soldier, armies marching, General Lee surrendering, and the nation rebuilding after Lincoln's vision. He speaks of the man becoming President, calling it something that could only happen in America. Overcome, he chokes slightly on his words. Babe watches his face throughout, initially tempted to laugh but unable to. She looks up at him, silent.
related_events: Babe points out Grant's Tomb to Longfellow
Babe and Longfellow discuss public perception of Grant's Tomb
Longfellow expresses awe at the sight of Grant's Tomb

name: Longfellow Speaks at Grant's Tomb
description: As they approach Grant's Tomb, Longfellow looks up at the monument and begins to speak. He describes an Ohio farm boy becoming a great soldier, sees armies marching, General Lee surrendering with a broken heart, and the beginning of a new nation. He speaks of the farm boy being inaugurated as President, his voice filled with awe. Babe watches his face as he talks, her initial impulse to laugh fading as she becomes absorbed in his words. Longfellow's voice falters, overcome with emotion, and he chokes slightly on his final words. 'Excuse me,' he says quietly. The scene fades out.
related_events: Longfellow envisions Grant's rise from farm boy to President
Babe observes Longfellow's emotional speech with fascination
Longfellow becomes emotionally overwhelmed during his speech

name: Longfellow and Babe Discuss the Opera Meeting
description: Longfellow tells Babe about the recent opera committee meeting, confirming he will continue as chairman. He explains that he offered to stay on if they agreed to lower ticket prices, reduce expenses, and begin broadcasting performances. Babe asks what the committee said, and Longfellow replies that they called him crazy, accusing him of wanting to run the opera like a grocery store. As they talk, Longfellow briefly shifts focus, complimenting Babe’s appearance and asking about her hairstyle. Two young women pass by, laughing about the nickname "Cinderella Man," which one calls ridiculous. After they leave, Longfellow asks Babe if she’s seen the newspapers, and she nods. He says he appreciates that she considers his feelings, and adds that he’d like to punch the reporter who wrote the article. Babe looks up, startled. Longfellow repeats the nickname quietly, then Babe suggests they go for a walk to enjoy the night air. Longfellow agrees, and they prepare to leave.
related_events: Longfellow confirms continued role as opera chairman
Longfellow reveals opera committee rejected his cost-cutting proposals
related_occasions: Opera Committee Meeting

name: Longfellow Defends Babe Against Mockery
description: After Longfellow mentions wanting to punch the writer of a negative article, two girls pass by, laughing. One of them says, "Isn't it a scream — 'Cinderella Man!' The dope!" The other replies, "I'd like to get my hooks into that guy." They walk away, still chattering. Longfellow stares after them, his expression dark. He says quietly, "If they were men, I'd knock their heads together." Babe remains silent, not looking up. Longfellow turns to her and asks, "Have you seen the papers?" She nods. He tells her he’d like to go to the newspaper and hit the man who wrote the story. Babe looks up, surprised. He repeats the nickname under his breath — "Cinderella Man" — then falls silent. Uncomfortable, Babe suggests they go for a walk. Longfellow agrees, and they stand to leave.
related_events: Longfellow expresses anger toward newspaper writer
Two passing girls mock Babe as "Cinderella Man"
Longfellow expresses desire to confront disrespectful girls

name: Longfellow and Babe: A Shift in Conversation
description: As they talk, Longfellow interrupts the discussion about the opera to tell Babe she looks pretty tonight. She laughs, then presses him for news about the meeting. He says the board called him crazy for wanting to lower prices, cut expenses, and broadcast the performances. Instead of continuing, he leans in and asks how she always wears her hair like that. Two young women pass by, laughing about the nickname "Cinderella Man," mocking Longfellow. He glares after them. Quietly, he says he would knock their heads together if they were men. Babe stays silent. Longfellow asks if she’s seen the papers, then says he admires her for caring about his feelings. He says he’d like to punch the reporter who wrote the article. Babe looks up, startled. He repeats the nickname under his breath. Uncomfortable, she suggests they walk the rest of the way since it’s a nice evening. He agrees, and they get up to leave.
related_events: Longfellow compliments Babe's appearance during conversation
Babe suggests walking together to change subject

name: Babe's Writer's Block and Mabel's Concern
description: Babe sits at a typewriter, staring at a sheet of paper with the words 'CINDERELLA MAN FIRE-EATING DEMON' typed on it. She rests her forehead on the typewriter carriage, motionless. Mabel Dawson, standing nearby at an easel, watches her quietly, then asks what is wrong. Babe quickly replies that nothing is the matter, but remains absorbed in her thoughts. Mabel approaches, noticing Babe hasn’t made progress on the page. She suggests they leave to meet friends at Joe's, but Babe suddenly stands and exclaims that she can’t write, lighting a cigarette in frustration. Mabel studies her with quiet understanding. The phone rings. Mabel answers, listens, and says, 'It's him—whatcha-ma-call-him—the Cinderella Man.' Babe immediately takes the phone, saying, 'Hello.'

Mabel Dawson observes Babe and inquires about her emotional state
Mabel observes Babe's typing progress and comments on lack of advancement
Babe resumes typing after pause
Babe expresses inability to write and shows emotional distress

name: Babe Takes the Call from the Cinderella Man
description: The phone rings. Mabel picks it up and listens. She says, 'Hello... Yes, she's here. Who wants her?' She pauses, then asks, 'Who?' After another pause, she says, 'Oh, yes. Yes, just a moment,' and covers the mouthpiece. She turns to Babe and says, 'It's him—whatcha-ma-call-him—the 'Cinderella Man.' The 'Cinderella Man!' Babe gets up quickly and takes the phone. 'Hello,' she says.

name: Longfellow Finds Babe Collapsed by the Tree
description: A girl stumbles from the shadows, staggering forward until she reaches a tree. She clutches it weakly and then collapses to the ground. Longfellow, seeing this, quickly rushes toward her. He kneels beside her and gently lifts her head, recognizing her as Babe Bennett. Her eyes open suddenly, and she looks up at him with feigned bewilderment, pretending to come around.
related_events: Girl staggers out of shadows and collapses near a tree
Longfellow rushes to the collapsed girl and lifts her head
Babe Bennett opens her eyes and pretends to regain consciousness

name: Babe Refuses Longfellow's Help After Fainting
description: After her eyes flutter open, Babe looks up at Longfellow with a dazed expression. He tells her she fainted, and she murmurs an apology, trying to push herself up. Longfellow reaches out to assist, but she waves him off, saying she’ll be fine. He invites her into his home, concern in his voice, but she declines, explaining she’s been walking all day looking for work and finally found a job starting tomorrow. She thanks him and takes a few unsteady steps away. After a short distance, she sways again, grabbing the iron fence to steady herself just as Longfellow starts toward her.
related_events: Babe Bennett apologizes and attempts to stand after fainting
Longfellow offers help and invites Babe into his home
Babe Bennett refuses Longfellow's invitation and explains her job search

name: Babe's Second Collapse and Longfellow's Response
description: After taking a few steps away, Babe Bennett suddenly weakens again, stumbling and falling against the iron fence, clutching it for support. Longfellow immediately rushes to her side. Looking around, he calls out, 'Hey, taxi!'
related_events: Babe Bennett pretends to weaken and collapses against the iron fence
Longfellow rushes to Babe Bennett after she collapses against the fence
Longfellow calls for a taxi after Babe's second collapse

name: Longfellow Tests the Echo with Walter
description: Longfellow stands at the top of the stairs and shouts down. An echo follows. He shouts again, louder, and the echo returns once more. Satisfied, he calls to Walter at the bottom of the stairs. Walter stops and looks up. Longfellow tells him to try. Walter hesitates, then lets out a soft, bird-like hoot. The echo answers. Longfellow tells him to be louder. Walter hoots again, increasing the volume each time as the echo repeats his sounds.
related_events: Longfellow shouts from the top of the stairs and observes an echo
Walter hesitantly produces a hoot at Longfellow's command

name: Longfellow Commands a Chorus of Echoes
description: A butler in a bathrobe appears at the sound of shouting, drawn from his room to investigate. Longfellow calls to him, and the butler, after a moment's hesitation, lets out a small, high-pitched squeak. At Longfellow's insistence, he tries again, louder. Another man-servant steps into view. Longfellow points to him, and the man responds with a deep, raspy hoot. Longfellow raises his arms like a conductor, urging them all to shout together. A cacophony of hoots, shrieks, and barks fills the space, each met with a clear echo. They do it once more, voices overlapping in noise and repetition. Longfellow surveys the scene, then turns sharply and walks back to his bedroom. The butler waits, then quietly dismisses the others. Once alone, he gives one final hoot before stepping away.
related_events: Butler emerges in bathrobe to investigate the noise
Butler participates in echo experiment with a squeak
Man-servant produces a raspy hoot at Longfellow's command

name: Longfellow Conducts an Echo Chorus
description: Longfellow stands at the top of the stairs and calls out, producing an echo. Walter, at the bottom, is prompted to try. He hoots timidly, then louder at Longfellow’s command, each sound met with a clear echo. A butler in a bathrobe appears, drawn by the noise. Longfellow instructs him to shout, and after a hesitant squeak, the butler complies with a louder call. Another servant emerges, and Longfellow directs him to join. The three produce a chorus of hoots, shrieks, and barks in overlapping bursts, the echoes reverberating with each round. Longfellow waves his arms as if conducting. After the second round, he pauses, surveys the group, and declares, 'Let that be a lesson to you,' before turning and walking back to his room. The butler ushers Walter and the other servant away. Once alone, the butler gives one final hoot, then exits quietly.
related_events: Household staff perform a coordinated chorus of hoots and echoes

name: The Butler's Final Hoot
description: After Longfellow turned and disappeared into his bedroom, the butler stepped forward, pointing to Walter and the man-servant. Go back to your room, both of you, he said, his voice sharp and commanding. The two servants hurried off without a word. Once he was sure no one was watching, the butler paused, then let out a single, quiet hoot into the empty hall. He murmured something to himself, barely audible, and then walked away, closing the door behind him.
related_events: Butler orders Walter and man-servant back to their rooms
Butler secretly delivers a final hoot before departing

name: Slide Down the Bannister and Touch the Statue
description: Longfellow exits his bedroom wearing a coat and hat, walks to the top of a grand staircase, and slides down the bannister. At the bottom, he reaches out and touches a statue before heading toward the door.
related_events: Longfellow slides down the bannister of a grand staircase
Longfellow touches a statue for good luck

name: Longfellow Confronts the Bodyguards
description: Longfellow exits his bedroom and descends the grand staircase, sliding down the bannister and touching a statue at the bottom before heading toward the door. His path is blocked by two burly figures. The first bodyguard asks if he’s going out. Longfellow confirms, questioning whether it’s allowed. The second bodyguard replies that it’s not—they explain they’ve been assigned by Mr. Cobb to stay with him at all times. Longfellow expresses discomfort with the constant surveillance. The first bodyguard apologizes, saying they’re only following orders. The second adds that their duties include getting him up in the morning and putting him to bed at night, but whatever they see, they won’t see anything. Longfellow smiles and remarks that’s going to be fun. The second bodyguard responds that some people like it. Longfellow pauses, then asks them to retrieve a trunk from a nearby room. The bodyguards agree and enter the closet. Longfellow calmly closes the door behind them and turns the key, locking them inside. They shout from within, protesting that they’re his bodyguards and he can’t do this. Unfazed, Longfellow whistles as he walks out.

The first bodyguard starts to draw a pistol, but the second slaps the weapon away and assures Longfellow they are ready to assist. Both men enter the closet to get the trunk. As soon as they are inside, Longfellow closes the door and turns the key, locking them in. The bodyguards shout from within, protesting that they are his bodyguards and he cannot leave them trapped. Longfellow remains calm, whistles to himself, and walks away through the door.

name: Morrow's Drunken Apology
description: Morrow, unsteady and clearly drunk, pushes through the crowd as Longfellow and Babe are heading out. A waiter tries to stop him, but he strides forward. Longfellow and Babe turn as Morrow stumbles toward them. He slurs his words, saying Longfellow neglected him and that he feels hurt. He jabs a finger at his chin, urging Longfellow to hit him—right there, hard. Longfellow doesn’t react, and after a beat, Morrow softens. He admits he knows when he’s been a fool, calling himself a skunk. He offers to eat a pack of postcards raw if they take him to a newsstand. Longfellow and Babe exchange small smiles. Morrow sways, nearly falling backward, but Longfellow grabs his collar and steadies him. Morrow laughs, calling the moment a magnificent deflation of smugness, and says Longfellow has added ten years to his life. He calls him a poet with a punch and declares he’ll be his guest forever. Longfellow thanks him but says he and Miss Dawson are going out to see the sights. Morrow insists he’ll show them sights they’ve never seen—Grant’s Tomb, the Statue of Liberty, the Leaning Tower of Pisa, even Mount Everest and the Pyramids. He invites Longfellow on a wild night across New York, promising to introduce him to every wit and half-wit in the city, a binge that would make Omar Khayyam look sober. Longfellow, puzzled, says that might be fun. Morrow, growing more animated, promises a night that will live in memory as a thing of beauty. He calls out for his hat, then stumbles off, shouting Latin phrases to no one in particular. He bumps into a woman, who snaps that he’s drunk. He agrees, unfazed. Back with Babe, Longfellow says they’ll probably see things if they go with Morrow. Babe looks at him, surprised, and says yes, they probably will.

He tells her he expected more from her, recalling a time when she would have taken on Corny Cobb without hesitation. Babe asks if the vacation would be with pay, and when Mac confirms, she casually tells him to leave four columns open on the front page for tomorrow’s paper. As she heads for the door, Mac calls after her, wanting to know what she’s going to do. She replies, 'Have lunch,' and walks out.
related_events: Editor Mac expresses disappointment in Babe Bennett

related_occasions: Newsroom Staff Briefing Led By Editor Mac

name: Babe Secures Deal and Promises Front-Page Story
description: The editor, Mac, berates the reporters and photographers gathered in the newsroom, frustrated by their lack of progress on the story about the newcomer who inherited the Semple fortune. As the others leave, Babe Bennett remains near the door, idly flicking a string, attempting to tie a knot in it like a cowboy with a rope. Mac turns to her, disappointed, but she interrupts, showing him the string trick. He ignores it, pressing her to deliver real results. Babe tells him she can get the story if he gives her a month’s vacation with pay. Mac agrees. She tells him to leave four columns open on the front page for her story tomorrow. Mac, energized, says he’ll keep the whole front page open and asks what she’s going to do. Babe replies, 'Have lunch,' and walks out. Mac watches her go, his expression bright with hope.

Babe Bennett announces front-page story for next day
Babe Bennett demonstrates string trick to Editor Mac
Babe Bennett departs for lunch after confrontation in newsroom
Editor Mac shows approval and optimism after Babe's commitment

name: Cobb's Introduction and Longfellow's Limerick
description: The three men sit around a table, sharing a meal, with Longfellow's tuba resting beside him. Cedar introduces Cobb as a man who once worked for Longfellow's uncle, describing him as a kind of buffer. Cobb interjects, calling himself a glorified doormat. Cedar explains that such a role was necessary to keep people and the press at bay, managing when the family should be seen and when they should not. As Cedar speaks, Longfellow appears distracted, lost in thought. He suddenly remarks that he can't think of a rhyme for Budington. Cobb asks why he should care. Longfellow replies that he enjoys finding rhymes for unusual names, then announces he has one for Cobb. He recites a limerick: 'There once was a man named Cobb, Who kept Semple away from the mob. Came the turn of the tide And Semple - he died - And now poor Cobb's out of a job!' Cobb responds dryly that it sounds like two weeks' notice, adding he's been fired in many ways but never in rhyme. Longfellow assures him the poem wasn't meant as a dismissal, and Cobb accepts this, noting it's different if it's just poetry.
related_events: Cedar introduces Cobb as Longfellow's uncle's former buffer
Longfellow attempts to create a rhyme for Budington
Longfellow recites a rhyming poem about Cobb
Cobb reacts to the rhymed poem with dry humor

name: Preparing for the Trip to New York
description: Cedar tells Longfellow it's time to go to New York. Longfellow asks when, and Cobb replies that they are leaving that afternoon at four o'clock. Longfellow expresses concern about not having suitcases, and Mrs. Meredith suggests borrowing a couple from Mrs. Simpson, who had used them for a trip to Niagara Falls the previous year. Longfellow admits he’s never been away from Mandrake Falls before and says he’s nervous, though he’d like to see Grant’s Tomb. Cedar shakes Longfellow’s hand, congratulates him on becoming one of the richest men in the country, and says they’ll meet him at the train. Cobb and Anderson say their goodbyes and leave with Cedar. Longfellow sits at the table, barely touching his lunch, while Mrs. Meredith tells him to eat.
related_events: Cedar informs Longfellow of his upcoming trip to New York
Cobb confirms the departure time for the trip
Mrs. Meredith suggests borrowing suitcases for the trip

name: Cedar Congratulates Longfellow and Departs
description: Cedar rose from the table, shook Longfellow's hand, and said, 'Congratulations, Mr. Deeds. You're one of the richest men in the country.' He turned to Mrs. Meredith, thanked her, and then joined Cobb and Anderson as they left the room. The three men walked out, leaving Longfellow and Mrs. Meredith behind.
related_events: Cedar congratulates Longfellow on becoming one of the richest men in the country
Cedar and Cobb bid farewell before departing

name: Mrs. Meredith Serves Coffee During the Meeting
description: Mrs. Meredith enters the room carrying coffee and pours a cup for each person at the table. The men pause briefly as she moves among them, the steam rising from the fresh coffee. The meal continues, with the conversation settling into a quieter rhythm as the group takes their drinks.
related_events: Mrs. Meredith serves coffee to the group

name: Mrs. Meredith Insists Longfellow Eat
description: After the others leave, Mrs. Meredith tells Longfellow to stay seated and finish his lunch, pointing out he hasn't touched his food. Longfellow begins to nibble at his meal, staring into space as he quietly processes the news of his sudden fortune.

Longfellow thoughtfully eats while reflecting on his fortune

name: Arrival in Mandrake Falls
description: Cobb, Cedar, and Anderson stand on the train platform in Mandrake Falls, surrounded by a quiet rural scene. Mail, newspapers, and freight are being loaded at one end. The three men, clearly out of place, face a welcome sign. Cobb reads the town's poem aloud: 'Welcome to Mandrake Falls - Where the scenery enthralls - Where no hardship e'er befalls - Welcome to Mandrake Falls.' He remarks that it's pretty. Cedar looks around and asks if this is really the town where Longfellow Deeds lives. Anderson assures him it is, confirming they checked thoroughly. Cobb spots an old man nearby and suggests they ask him. They approach a small brick building covered in ivy, where the elderly rail agent fiddles with packages, occasionally stepping inside without finishing his conversations.
related_events: Cobb, Cedar, and Anderson arrive at Mandrake Falls train platform
Cobb reads the Mandrake Falls welcome poem aloud
Cedar questions whether they are in the right town

name: Cedar and Cobb Question the Rail Agent
description: Cobb notices an old man near a small brick building covered in ivy and suggests they ask him for help. The group approaches the ticket and freight office where the rail agent is puttering around a pile of packages. Cedar greets him, but the man only looks up briefly and calls them 'neighbors' before picking up a package and going inside. He returns moments later and resumes his work. Cedar asks if he knows a man named Longfellow Deeds. The agent replies that everyone knows Deeds, then turns and walks back into the building. Cedar and Cobb exchange glances as the man reappears, seemingly unaware of their presence. Cedar repeats that they need to get in touch with Deeds, emphasizing it's important. The agent nods, calls Deeds a fine and democratic fellow, and says they won't have any trouble, then carries another package inside. Frustrated, Cedar suggests trying someone else. Cobb insists they stay. When the agent emerges again and begins to walk away, Cobb steps forward, grabs his arm, and gently forces him to sit on a packing crate. He reminds the man they’ve already spoken and says they’ve come from New York to find Deeds. The agent pulls his arm away, saying there's no need to get rough. Cobb, holding his composure, asks once more where Deeds lives. The agent looks up and says, 'Who?'
related_events: Cobb spots the rail agent and suggests asking for help
The group approaches the rail agent at the ticket office
Cedar greets the rail agent and asks about Longfellow Deeds

name: Cobb Confronts the Evasive Rail Agent
description: Cobb, growing increasingly frustrated with the old rail agent's repeated disappearances and apparent forgetfulness, grabs the man by the arm as he tries to retreat into the building again. He guides the agent to a small packing case and firmly sets him down, insisting they are the same men who spoke with him moments ago. The agent claims he never forgets a face, but when Cobb demands to know where Longfellow Deeds lives, the old man asks again who they are looking for. Cobb, refusing to let him escape, holds his ground and presses for a direct answer.
related_events: Cobb becomes exasperated with the rail agent's evasive behavior
Rail agent feigns forgetfulness and avoids answering directly
Cobb demands the rail agent provide information about Deeds' residence
Cobb restrains the rail agent to prevent him from leaving

name: Anderson Secures the Agent's Help
description: Cobb turns away in disgust, folding his arms. Anderson steps forward and asks the rail agent where Longfellow Deeds lives. The old man looks up slowly and says he knows exactly where Deeds is. He adds that they should have just asked instead of carrying on. Without waiting for a reply, he grabs a set of keys from his pocket, walks over to a dusty car parked nearby, and opens the door. He gestures for them to follow, saying he’ll drive them there himself.
related_events: Cobb expresses disgust and turns away

name: Longfellow Rejects Opera Investment and Confronts Estate Claim
description: Longfellow enters the room and apologizes for the delay, explaining that opera representatives had asked him to invest $180,000. He tells Hallor and Cedar that he turned them down. Hallor then brings up his client's claim on the estate. Longfellow, distracted by his valet Walter presenting a formal tailcoat, reacts with disbelief, calling it a 'monkey suit' and refusing to wear it. Walter kneels to help him with his trousers, but Longfellow orders him to get up, insisting he doesn't need anyone holding the ends of his pants. After reprimanding Walter, Longfellow turns back to Hallor, who reiterates that Mrs. Semple is legally entitled to one-third of the estate—about $7 million. Hallor suggests she might settle for one million. Cedar interjects that any settlement talks should go through him, but Longfellow cuts in, telling Hallor to leave and refusing to let him go to Cedar's office. He says he doesn't like Hallor's face and finds it suspicious that someone would settle for so little. Hallor warns him not to get tough, reminding him they have letters. Longfellow pulls the bell cord, stating that one advantage of being rich is that things happen when you ring. He tells Hallor that when the servant arrives, he will be shown to the door.
related_events: Longfellow refuses opera funding request
Hallor raises client's claim on estate

name: Longfellow Rejects Formal Attire and Valet's Assistance
description: As Longfellow enters, his valet Walter holds up a full dress suit, asking if he should prepare tails for the evening. Longfellow reacts with disbelief, calling it a 'monkey suit' and refusing to wear it. Walter then kneels, holding the ends of the trousers to help Longfellow dress. Longfellow demands he get up, saying he doesn’t want anyone holding the ends of his pants. Walter rises and apologizes. Longfellow repeats his order, telling Walter never to kneel again. He expresses discomfort with the formal clothing and the servile behavior, rejecting both.

Longfellow rejects formal wear and servant assistance

name: Longfellow Rejects Settlement and Orders Hallor Out
description: Hallor tells Longfellow that Mrs. Semple is legally entitled to one-third of the estate, which amounts to about seven million dollars. He quickly adds that he believes he can settle the claim for one million. Cedar interjects, instructing Hallor to discuss any settlement terms with him at the office. Hallor refuses, but Longfellow interrupts, telling Hallor he will not go to anyone’s office—he is going out the door. Hallor protests, saying Longfellow is making a mistake. Longfellow replies that he doesn’t like Hallor’s face and finds it suspicious that someone would accept a million dollars when they could claim seven million. He expresses disappointment that Cedar, whom he considers a smart man, doesn’t see the same flaw. Hallor starts to respond, but Longfellow walks to the bell cord and pulls it. He says one advantage of being rich is that when you ring a bell, things happen. He informs Hallor that when the servant arrives, he will be shown to the door. Hallor warns that acting tough won’t help, but Longfellow remains firm. Hallor then states, 'You know, we've got letters.'

name: Longfellow Orders Hallor's Removal from the Residence

He then walks to the bell cord, pulls it, and announces that one advantage of being rich is that when you ring a bell, things happen. Without further explanation, he states his intention to support Longfellow genuinely. Longfellow listens without response, the room quiet between them.

name: Walter Helps Longfellow with His Coat

name: Mrs. Meredith Welcomes Visitors and Explains Mr. Deeds' Absence
description: Mrs. Meredith opens the door to find Cedar, Cobb, and Anderson standing outside, with an older man following behind them. She greets them warmly and invites them in. When asked if Mr. Deeds is home, she replies that he is not, explaining that he is at the park arranging for a bazaar to raise money for the fire engine. She offers the visitors tea, then lemonade, but they decline. She mentions that she is Mr. Deeds' housekeeper and begins to describe his work, noting that while he co-owns the Tallow Works, he earns most of his income from writing poetry on postcards. She picks up one of the postcards and reads a sentimental verse aloud. As she finishes, a dog rushes in, scratching at the door and whining. Mrs. Meredith goes to open it, stepping outside briefly before returning, saying, "They've been waiting a long while," as Longfellow Deeds enters behind her.

name: Mrs. Meredith Reveals Mr. Deeds' Poetry
description: Cedar asks Mrs. Meredith about Mr. Deeds' occupation. She explains that while he co-owns the Tallow Works with Jim Mason, he earns most of his money from writing poetry on postcards for holidays like Christmas, Easter, and birthdays. She picks up one of the postcards from a desk and reads it aloud: "When you've nowhere to turn - and you're filled with doubt - Don't stand in midstream, hesitating, For you know that your mother's heart cries out - 'I'm waiting, my boy, I'm waiting.'" She calls the verse beautiful and asks if the men agree. Cobb stares in disbelief. A dog rushes in, scratching at the door, and Mrs. Meredith opens it and steps outside. As she leaves, she says, "They've been waiting a long while." Longfellow Deeds enters behind her. She introduces the visitors, and Cedar steps forward, presenting his card and identifying himself as John Cedar of the New York law firm Cedar, Cedar, Cedar and Budington. Longfellow reads the name on the card and smiles, saying Budington must feel like an awful stranger. Cobb watches, unamused.

Mrs. Meredith describes Mr. Deeds' poetry and reads a postcard poem aloud

name: The Dog Signals Deeds' Return

name: Mr. Deeds Meets the Legal Team
description: Mrs. Meredith returns through the doorway, followed by Longfellow Deeds. She says the visitors have been waiting a long while. Deeds looks at the group and asks who they are. Cedar stands and greets him formally, introducing himself as John Cedar of the New York law firm Cedar, Cedar, Cedar and Budington. He hands Deeds a card. name: Cedar and Cobb Deliver the Inheritance News
description: Cedar asks Longfellow Deeds about his identity and family, confirming that he is the nephew of Martin W. Semple. Longfellow calmly affirms his relation to the late Semple, speaking in a quiet, steady manner. Cedar then announces that Semple has passed away and left Longfellow a fortune of twenty million dollars. name: Babe and Longfellow Share a Quiet Moment About Love and Hometowns
description: Babe brings up something Longfellow once said—that she was a lady in distress. He brushes it off, but she presses gently, wanting to know what he meant. He doesn’t answer directly. Instead, after a pause, he asks if she’s engaged. She smiles faintly and says no, then turns the question back to him. His voice answers quietly—no. She observes that he doesn’t seem to go out with many girls. He agrees, saying he hasn’t. She wonders why, suggesting he must have met plenty of society girls he liked. He says he hasn’t particularly liked any of them, adding they all seem to have the St. Vitus Dance—then quickly adds, except her. He reflects that people here work so hard at living they forget how to live. He recalls walking past tall buildings the night before and thinking about Thoreau—how they’ve built grand palaces but forgotten to create noblemen to fill them. He says he’d rather have Mandrake Falls. Babe responds that she’s from a small town too, about the same size. Longfellow is surprised and interested. She remembers it fondly—a row of poplar trees on Main Street, the clean smell, the quiet. She used to fish with her father, who reminded her of Longfellow. He didn’t talk much, but once told her, “No matter what happens, honey, don’t complain.” He played in the town band. Longfellow mentions he plays the tuba. She knows—he asks what her father played. The drums. He taught her a little. She can play “Swanee River.” Longfellow asks if she’ll play it for him. She smiles and says she will.

name: Babe and Longfellow Discuss Society and Connection
description: Babe asks Longfellow why he doesn’t go out with girls, noting he hasn’t seemed to engage much with the women around them. He replies that he hasn’t met anyone he particularly likes, describing the people in the city as awkward, as if they all have the St. Vitus Dance, though he quickly adds that he doesn’t mean her. He says people here work so hard at living that they forget how to live. He recalls walking past tall buildings the night before and thinking about a quote from Thoreau—how the city has built grand palaces but never created the noblemen to fill them. He says he’d rather have Mandrake Falls. Babe responds that she’s also from a small town, about as small as his. Longfellow is surprised, and a sense of connection forms between them. Babe begins to reminisce about her childhood, describing the row of poplar trees on Main Street and how the town always smelled fresh. She remembers fishing with her father, who reminded her of Longfellow in the way he spoke and carried himself. She recalls sitting quietly with him by the water, holding the fishing line, and sometimes kissing him for no reason. He rarely spoke, but once told her, 'No matter what happens, honey, don’t complain.' Longfellow says her father sounded like a worthwhile person. Babe adds that her father played drums in the town band. Longfellow mentions he plays the tuba. Babe says she learned to play some drums from him and can play 'Swanee River.' Longfellow smiles and says he’d like to hear it.

He thought about how the city had built many grand palaces but had not created the kind of people who should live in them. Later, sitting with Babe, he told her that he would rather have Mandrake Falls than this place. He spoke of the city's people, how they seemed to work so hard at living that they forgot how to live.

name: Babe and Longfellow's Musical Duet in the Moonlight
description: Babe knelt beside the bushes, using two slender branches as drumsticks, tapping out a rhythm on a low tree stump. She began to sing 'Swanee River,' her voice soft but clear, her movements playful. When she finished, Longfellow shook his head with an exaggerated frown, feigning disappointment. She laughed and challenged him to do better. He straightened up, confident, and said he could sing 'Humoresque.' Babe raised an eyebrow, skeptical, and bet that he didn’t actually know the tune. Without hesitation, Longfellow proposed they perform together—she could sing 'Swanee River' again while he sang 'Humoresque' in counterpoint. Babe agreed, but only if he could actually carry the melody. She started singing first, her voice rising into the night air, and after a moment, Longfellow joined in, his voice weaving around hers in a careful, overlapping harmony. description: Cedar stands beside Longfellow as tailors adjust a suit on him, and suggests that granting Power of Attorney would simplify matters and shield him from constant requests by salesmen, politicians, and moochers. description: Longfellow suddenly remembers a pending task and turns to Cobb. 'Oh, did you send that telegram to Jim Mason?' Cobb hesitates, then pulls a written message from his pocket. name: Longfellow Confronts Mockery at the Writers' Table
description: At a round table in the restaurant, the group of writers turns their attention to Longfellow. Bill asks how he writes his poetry. Henaberry leans in, curious about where he finds inspiration. Longfellow answers hesitantly, clearly uneasy. Morrow remarks that his publishers must be frustrated with how slowly he works, and Longfellow offers a weak laugh. Babe watches him closely, unsure if he senses the tone shifting around them. Brookfield then asks about his writing process, and Longfellow explains he writes poetry on commission. Brookfield calls the idea brilliant, his voice laced with amusement. Henaberry follows up, asking if he has any strange habits while writing. Longfellow says he plays the tuba during composition. Morrow cuts in, joking that playing the harmonica never helped anyone write a poem. Brookfield asks if Longfellow carries around his poems on postcards, as he’s heard. Longfellow pauses. Henaberry feigns surprise that he doesn’t have any with him. Brookfield and Henaberry exchange glances, then pretend to eagerly request autographed copies. Bill chimes in, supporting the request. Henaberry suggests Longfellow recite one of his poems instead, and the others join in, urging him to perform a Mother’s Day poem for the table. Longfellow looks around at their faces, the laughter barely concealed. He sits up straight, his voice calm but firm, and speaks in defense of his work and the sincerity behind it. He tells them they don’t understand what it means to create from the heart. Then, without another word, he stands, pushes his chair in, and announces he is leaving. Babe rises with him, and the two walk away as the group falls silent.
